title: The oxygen cold trap in protoplanetary discs
html:
Abstract:The diffusive transport of oxygen in protoplanetary discs followed by sequestration into ice in the midplane, a process known as the cold trap, can substantially alter the chemical environment where planets form. This paper presents a new time-dependent modelling framework that allows us to consistently simulate kinetic gas-phase chemistry, ice growth and desorption, turbulent diffusive mixing, and gravitational settling of icy particles with a changing particle size distribution over million-year timescales in one-dimensional vertical columns. Applying our model to a T Tauri disc across radii from 1 to 100 au reveals that vertical cold trapping becomes an effective mechanism once the diffusion-to-settling timescale ratio exceeds unity, simultaneously driving the gas-phase C/O up toward unity, and the gas-phase C/H down, by up to two orders of magnitude at large distances. All models feature the development of an upward counter-flux due to the turbulent up-whirling of icy particles followed by ice sublimation above the horizontal icelines, which brings the cold trapping to a halt and eventually establishes a relaxed vertical structure after about $10^4$ to $10^6$ yr, depending on the radial distance. The ice formation leads to a strongly peaked size distribution around 1 mic, which contains the majority of the condensed mass in the disc after ice formation, and changes the dynamical behaviour of the grains substantially. We conclude that the vertical cold trap can provide an important part of the explanation why evolved discs observed with ALMA often show high C/O ratios as inferred from strong emissions from hydrocarbon molecules in the outer disc, such as C2H and c-C3H2. However, in none of our models does the C/O ratio exceed unity, which is a consequence of CO-blocking, a chemical process where water molecules naturally stop forming once C/O approaches unity.
